# 12 · Metrics endpoint: Prometheus counters, timing, /metrics and /healthz

*Sample output: what the model solution actually produces, on the input shown.*

## The main problem: a metrics store and an endpoint

Record some work. Counters take optional labels; `timed` feeds a summary:

```python
m = Metrics()
m.inc("jobs_total")
m.inc("http_requests_total", {"method": "GET", "path": "/api/users", "code": "200"})
m.inc("http_requests_total", {"code": "200", "method": "GET", "path": "/api/users"})
#      ^ the SAME series as the line above: same labels, different order
m.inc("http_requests_total", {"code": "500", "path": "/api/orders", "method": "POST"})
m.inc("bytes_written_total", value=4096)
m.observe("job_seconds", 0.25)          # two explicit observations, so the
m.observe("job_seconds", 0.75)          # sample output stays reproducible

with timed(m, "scrape_seconds"):        # the real timer: duration is measured
    do_work()
```

`render()` produces Prometheus text exposition format:

```text
# TYPE bytes_written_total counter
bytes_written_total 4096.0
# TYPE http_requests_total counter
http_requests_total{code="200",method="GET",path="/api/users"} 2.0
http_requests_total{code="500",method="POST",path="/api/orders"} 1.0
# TYPE jobs_total counter
jobs_total 1.0
# TYPE job_seconds summary
job_seconds_sum 1.0
job_seconds_count 2
# TYPE scrape_seconds summary
scrape_seconds_sum <measured>
scrape_seconds_count 1
```

Reading that: the two `/api/users` increments landed on ONE series at 2.0, even though the
second call passed the same labels in a different order — they're sorted into a tuple key,
so label order carries no meaning, exactly as in Prometheus itself. Had they not been
sorted you would get two half-counted series and a graph that silently understates traffic.
Each metric family gets a single `# TYPE` line, and output is sorted,
so two scrapes of unchanged state diff cleanly. A summary renders as two samples, `_sum`
and `_count`: fixed memory per series however many observations arrive, at the cost of no
real percentiles later. `scrape_seconds_sum` is the measured duration, replaced here with
a placeholder so this page doesn't change on every run.

Labels are escaped on the way out, because a value may contain quotes or newlines:

```text
# TYPE errors_total counter
errors_total{msg="he said \"no such file\"\nretrying",path="C:\\logs"} 1.0
```

Reading that: backslashes are escaped before quotes, never after — do it the other way and
the backslashes you just inserted get escaped a second time, corrupting every scrape.

## The main problem: serving it over HTTP

```python
server = make_server(metrics, {"disk": lambda: True, "queue": lambda: True})
threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
base = f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_address[1]}"      # port 0: the OS picks a free one
```

Four real requests against the running server (the port is an OS-assigned one, shown
here as `<port>`):

```text
GET http://127.0.0.1:<port>/metrics   -> 200 text/plain; version=0.0.4
    body: 13 lines of exposition format, as above

GET http://127.0.0.1:<port>/healthz   -> 200 application/json
    body: {"status": "ok"}

GET http://127.0.0.1:<port>/healthz   -> 503 application/json      # the sick server
    body: {"status": "fail", "failed": ["db", "queue"]}

GET http://127.0.0.1:<port>/nope      -> 404 text/plain
    body: 'not found'
```

Reading that: `/healthz` returns 503, not 500, and names which checks failed — `db` raised
a ConnectionError and `queue` returned False, and both count as failures. A check that
crashes must never become a 500: a 500 is indistinguishable from the endpoint itself being
broken, and it loses the body that tells you which dependency to look at. The list is
sorted, so an alert on the body text doesn't flap. Checks run per request, because a
cached answer is not health.

## The variant: reading a scrape back

Two scrapes 60 seconds apart. Note the `/api/orders` counter went DOWN, which only
happens when the process restarted:

```text
# HELP http_requests_total Total requests.
# TYPE http_requests_total counter
http_requests_total{method="GET",path="/api/users"} 1000
http_requests_total{method="POST",path="/api/orders"} 40
http_requests_total{path="/search",query="a,b"} 7
process_start_time_seconds 1.789e+09

--- 60 seconds later ---

# TYPE http_requests_total counter
http_requests_total{method="GET",path="/api/users"} 1600
http_requests_total{method="POST",path="/api/orders"} 10
http_requests_total{path="/search",query="a,b"} 7
process_start_time_seconds 1.789e+09
```

`parse_exposition(...)` then `counter_rate(prev, curr, seconds=60)`:

```python
len(parse_exposition(scrape_1)) -> 4   # comment lines ignored

counter_rate(prev, curr, 60) ->
    http_requests_total{method="GET",path="/api/users"}     10.0000/s
    http_requests_total{method="POST",path="/api/orders"}    0.1667/s
    http_requests_total{path="/search",query="a,b"}          0.0000/s
    process_start_time_seconds                               0.0000/s
```

Reading that: `/api/users` climbed 1000 -> 1600 over 60s, so 10/s. `/api/orders` fell from
40 to 10, which a counter cannot do — the process restarted, so the increase is taken as
the current value (10 over 60s, 0.1667/s) rather than a nonsensical -0.5/s. Every alert
built on a rate depends on that rule; without it, each deploy emits a huge negative spike.
The unchanged series reports 0.0/s, and `query="a,b"` survives with its comma intact,
because label values are parsed as quoted strings rather than split on commas.
